The collector’s notebook

A mineral collection with a point of view.

Black Michael Collection · November 09, 2026

Build a personal mineral collection around the specimens you enjoy and the information you can preserve.

Begin with what draws you in

Your first collection does not need to cover every mineral or come with a grand plan. Start with a question: are you drawn to color, crystal form, a place, or a particular kind of display? A small, focused selection can be more satisfying than a shelf filled without intention.

Look beyond the first photograph

Ask for views from more than one side and a photograph with a ruler. Make sure you understand the specimen’s dimensions, how it sits, and what is included. A close-up can make a small piece appear much larger than it is.

Keep the information with the specimen

Save the original label, seller’s description and any locality information. Record the purchase date and your own photographs. Separate documented information from a seller’s attribution or an unanswered question; a clear record is more useful than an overconfident label.

Ask about condition

Before buying, ask about repairs, restoration, attached pieces and areas of damage. Request close-ups of anything you want to understand. The aim is to make a choice with a clear picture of the actual specimen.

Choose display before cleaning

Think about a stable display location away from accidental knocks. Ask for handling and storage guidance for that particular specimen. Avoid choosing a cleaning method until you know what the specimen is and how it should be handled.

Leave room to learn

A collection can change direction as your interests develop. Keep notes on what you enjoy, what you would like to see in person, and which questions you want to ask at your next mineral show.
